title: Garbage collector fused with a columnar compressor for old generation
idea: Combine the generational GC's copying/promotion phase with compression: objects promoted to the old generation are packed into per-class columnar blocks (field-transposed, delta- and dictionary-encoded), and a read barrier decompresses on access through a small decoded-object cache.
why: Managed heaps (Java, Go, JS, Python) run at 2-5x live data with highly redundant fields; a 2-3x old-gen shrink is plausible.

title: Producer-side compression: NICs and SSDs write memory pre-compressed
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: publish the memory controller's compressed-line format as a standard and let NICs, SSD controllers and accelerators DMA data already in that format, so the uncompressed copy never occupies DRAM; the CPU's controller decompresses only when a core actually touches the line.
why: I/O buffers, page cache and receive rings are 10-30% of server DRAM; storing them compressed from birth gives ~1.5-2x on that slice and saves write bandwidth.

title: Matryoshka weights that shrink themselves under memory pressure
idea: Inverts 'a deployed model has a fixed size': nested-width training lets a serving node evict the trailing slices of every weight matrix when DRAM is tight and reload them when it is not, trading a few points of quality for 2-4x less weight memory in real time.
why: An elastic footprint lets fleets size DRAM for average demand instead of peak.

title: Apollo core-rope weaver: frozen weights in via-programmed ROM chiplets
idea: Apollo's flight software was literally woven into core-rope ROM. Production model weights that won't change for a year are mask-programmed into dense, multi-bit, stackable via-ROM chiplets on a mature node and co-packaged beside the accelerator. HBM then holds only KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are 50-80% of inference HBM. ROM needs no capacitor, no refresh and no EUV, and it can be made in 28-40 nm US fabs. That frees most HBM for KV cache and attacks capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Seed-generated weights from LFSR banks in mature-node logic
idea: IFR: weights that occupy no memory. Constraint: memory chips need W, Hf and Ta but plain logic need not, so trade memory for logic: each 8x8 weight block is stored as a 16-bit LFSR seed plus four small coefficients, and thousands of LFSR+MAC units regenerate weights at line rate in 65-130 nm CMOS wired in Al-Cu with Ti/TiN barriers and TiSi2 contacts.
why: ~3-4 bits per weight cuts weight DRAM 4-5x versus BF16 using only Si, Al, Cu, Ti, N and O.

title: Derivable pages: kernel drops memory it can recompute from recipes
idea: Box: recompute × OS kernel × page × memory pressure × registered recipe handle. Applications mark pages as derived (decompressed libraries, parsed configs, dequantized weights, JIT code) with a callback; under pressure the kernel discards them like clean page cache and re-runs the recipe on fault instead of swapping.
why: A large share of anonymous memory is a cache of cheap computation; making it reclaimable cuts provisioned DRAM 10–30% with no swap I/O.

title: Torpor mode: idle containers hibernate to NV, keeping heartbeat pages
idea: Like animals in torpor keeping only vital functions, idle containers and serverless functions are snapshotted to CXL-attached persistent flash in milliseconds, leaving only profiled heartbeat pages (timers, socket state) in DRAM, with userfaultfd lazy restore on wake.
why: Warm-but-idle instances dominate serverless DRAM; 5-10x more warm instances per GB, and state survives power loss.

title: Appliance energy labels: 'R0 zero-refresh' procurement class for memory
idea: Borrowed from ENERGY STAR and EU appliance labels: U.S. federal and CHIPS-funded datacenter procurement adopts an 'R0' rating for servers whose memory hierarchy spends no power on refresh (SRAM, ROM, NVM or refresh-free ephemeral tiers), with a 10-15% price preference and published watts per idle GB.
why: Creates a guaranteed early market for refresh-free, less-DRAM architectures; refresh is 16-33% of idle memory power across the fleet it targets.

title: Dekatron-style ferroelectric counting capacitor tracks page hotness
idea: Like dekatron tubes that stepped one state per pulse, a sub-coercive ferroelectric capacitor switches a fixed fraction of its domains on each access pulse, accumulating a nonvolatile count. One capacitor per 64 KB region sits in a small university-built HZO array beside the memory controller and is read and reset each epoch to drive tier migration.
why: Tiering saves DRAM only if hotness is known; a one-capacitor analog counter gives per-region access counts with no SRAM counter tables, enabling 30-50% smaller fast tiers.

title: Encode-heavy, decode-cheap memory codec trained by idle cores
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: reads outnumber writes ~3-10x, so use an asymmetric codec: pages are written raw, then idle cores or a background engine re-encode warm pages with expensive search (optimal parsing plus per-page tANS tables), while the read path is a fixed two-stage table-lookup decoder with deterministic ~10 ns latency.
why: Gets entropy-coder ratios (2.5-3.5x) at BDI-class read latency on warm data; 1.5-2x effective DRAM on read-mostly working sets.

title: Append-only log memory on SLC flash with DRAM write buffer
idea: Worsen: send random small writes to flash and kill it in weeks. Flip: make memory log-structured, with writes coalesced in a small DRAM buffer and appended sequentially to SLC flash, random reads served directly from flash, and garbage collection run in idle time.
why: Cost: SLC at about $0.15/GB with practical endurance gives 60-100x cheaper capacity for read-mostly working sets.

title: Ferroelectric fast checkpoints let exclusive tasks time-share one DRAM
idea: Mutually exclusive vehicle workloads (parking, highway, cabin assistant) each checkpoint their whole state into AlScN FeRAM in milliseconds, using ns polarization switching. The next task is then swapped in, so one small DRAM serves several tasks over time instead of each owning its own. Wurtzite polarization survives 125 C for 10 years.
why: DRAM is sized for the peak task rather than the sum, for 2-4x less DRAM per vehicle.

title: Heat-annealed self-healing flash becomes a write-tolerant DRAM extension
idea: Use the 125 C ambient plus brief on-die heater pulses to keep annealing trapped charge out of NAND tunnel oxide (the self-healing flash effect), pushing SLC endurance toward 1e8 cycles. Flash can then act as a swap tier for warm pages behind a small DRAM.
why: Turns heat from enemy into feature: DRAM can shrink 2-4x behind a high-endurance flash tier in hot environments.

title: Tungsten-free 3D NAND with silicided-poly wordlines as KV overflow tier
idea: IFR: unlimited KV overflow with no chokepoint materials. Closest: 3D charge-trap NAND built with TiSi2-clad doped poly-Si wordlines instead of W replacement gates, accepting higher wordline RC through shorter blocks, read in large sequential KV pages behind a small DRAM cache.
why: Makes the DRAM-offload tier itself W-free while enabling ~10x less DRAM for long-context serving.

title: Layer-lockstep weight broadcast: each server holds one-sixteenth of model
idea: Imposed limit: no server may store more than 1/16 of a model's weights. Sixteen inference servers each keep one shard in DRAM and take turns multicasting their layers over an optical broadcast bus; every server runs its own batch in lockstep, using each layer as it streams past and then discarding it, like a choir reading from one shared score.
why: Weights are 50-80% of inference DRAM; cluster-wide weight DRAM falls ~16x in exchange for multicast bandwidth (a few hundred GB/s), cutting how much DRAM each server needs.

title: Insect-swarm forking: cache-line copy-on-write for thousand-agent fan-out
idea: From swarms where thousands of agents share nearly identical state: the memory controller supports 64-byte-granular copy-on-write through an indirection table, so forking an agent, VM or KV prefix shares every identical line and allocates only the lines that actually diverge.
why: Page-level CoW wastes 4 KB per changed line; line-level sharing makes 1,000 forks cost ~1.1 copies, cutting DRAM, and its fab water, 10x+ for fan-out workloads.

title: Compile long shared contexts into adapters instead of KV
idea: Reverse context->weights: documents reused across many requests (codebases, manuals, policies) are distilled offline into a small LoRA or a trained KV 'cartridge' of a few MB, so requests stop holding a 100k-token KV cache for the same text.
why: KV for repeated long contexts drops 10-100x: a few MB of cartridge instead of GBs of KV per concurrent request.

title: Pod-wide HBM borrowing over the scale-up fabric
idea: In a 72-GPU NVLink-class domain, each GPU exposes its idle HBM through the fabric. KV overflow and cold weights spill to a neighbor's HBM at about 1 TB/s, so no single GPU has to be provisioned for worst-case context length. Provisioning moves from the chip scale to the pod scale.
why: Provisioning for the pod average instead of each GPU's peak needs 25-40% less HBM per accelerator at the same SLOs.

title: Net metering for RAM: credits for ballooning memory back
idea: Like rooftop-solar owners selling surplus to the grid, cloud tenants run a balloon agent that hands unused RAM back to the provider in real time and earns per-GB-minute credits at the current spot price, redeemable when they need to grow.
why: Turns idle tenant DRAM (often 30%+) into reusable supply through incentive design rather than new silicon.

title: Controller-side pointer high-bit extraction into per-page region tags
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out: the memory controller detects 64-bit words whose upper 24 bits equal a per-page 'region tag' (pointers into the same heap region), strips those bits and packs eight 40-bit pointers into a 40-byte slot, restoring them on read with one mux stage. It is hardware compressed-oops for every language, not just the JVM.
why: Pointer-heavy heaps (graph DBs, Go/Java, kernels, B-trees) are 30-60% pointers; 20-35% capacity gain on those pages at ~1-cycle decode.

title: Street-sweeper routes: LLM weight reads double as refresh
idea: Borrowed from municipal sweeper routes that cover every street on a fixed cycle: during decode every weight row is read once per token (~10-30 ms), so the controller orders weight fetches as a route covering every row inside the retention window and disables explicit refresh for weight banks; when the server idles the banks may decay and are reloaded from flash on wake.
why: Weights are the largest DRAM region on inference servers; zero refresh power and 10-20% bandwidth recovered, so fewer or smaller stacks deliver the same throughput.

title: Race-car telemetry decay: multi-resolution rings that downsample in place
idea: From F1 and flight telemetry with fixed memory: metric and trace stores keep a fixed-size ring per series in which a background engine merges older samples into progressively coarser buckets (mean, min, max, quantile sketch), so memory per series is constant regardless of retention.
why: Time-series stores grow linearly with retention; exponential decimation makes them logarithmic, cutting DRAM 10x+ for long windows.

title: Radar MTI cancellers: store only frame-to-frame activation changes
idea: Copy radar moving-target-indicator cancellers, which stored one sweep in a delay line and subtracted the next: video and streaming-sensor models keep a reference activation map and store and propagate only entries whose change exceeds a threshold, as sparse deltas, refreshing the reference every N frames.
why: Static-camera and robot streams change <10% of activations per frame; activation memory and bandwidth drop 5-20x for video-analytics fleets.

title: Retired GPUs become attention-computing KV-cache servers
idea: Combine previous-generation accelerators (HBM2-era parts on non-EUV processes) with attention offload: the new GPU ships query vectors over the network, the retired GPU holds long-context KV in its HBM and returns attention outputs, so only small vectors cross the link.
why: Turns stranded HBM2 into extra KV capacity without new DRAM and frees 50-70% of new GPUs' HBM for weights and batch.

title: Swap HBM weight storage for read-only stacked NAND beside smaller HBM
idea: Substitute HBM with high-bandwidth stacked NAND for the read-only tier. Inference weights do not change for months, so a wide, many-plane NAND die stack on the same interposer streams them into SRAM in 4-16 KB pages, and HBM shrinks to KV cache and activations. Endurance does not matter because weights are written only at model deployment.
why: Weights are 40-70% of accelerator memory. NAND is ~10x cheaper per bit and needs no EUV for capacity, so HBM per accelerator falls ~2x, and the HBM TSV tax falls with it.

title: Swap per-host duplicate pages for one fleet-shared CXL read-only copy
idea: Substitute per-host duplicates with one rack copy. Read-only pages (kernel text, shared libraries, container layers, model weights, JIT code caches) are hashed across the rack, one canonical copy is stored in a CXL-switched memory appliance and mapped read-only into every host, and writes copy-on-write into local DRAM.
why: Same-host dedup (KSM) misses cross-host duplication. Rack-wide single copies recover an estimated 5-15% of fleet DRAM.

title: CXL switch holds a rack-wide page dedup table
idea: Combine the CXL switch's address-routing tables (mature-node switch silicon) with a global content-hash index: identical pages across every host in a rack (OS images, runtimes, model weights) are stored once in pooled memory and mapped read-only into each host, with copy-on-write on modification.
why: Cross-host duplication in a rack far exceeds per-host duplication, so 20-40% of pooled capacity could be saved.

title: Lending library: rack-wide shared read-only NV pages mapped in place
idea: Like a public library replacing private bookshelves, OS images, shared libraries, container layers and model weights live once in a rack-level persistent CXL memory appliance mapped read-only (DAX) into every host, so no host spends DRAM caching its own copy.
why: Removes per-host duplicates of identical read-mostly data (often 10-30% of DRAM) across 32-64 hosts.

title: Content-hashed singleton cache for model weights across a rack
idea: Inference hosts each keep 10-30 model checkpoints in host DRAM for fast swapping, mostly the same popular open weights. Hash each 2 MB weight page and keep one physical copy in a rack CXL appliance, mapped read-only into every host; LoRA adapters and private fine-tunes stay local.
why: Host-side model caches shrink 10-30x per rack (N identical copies down to 1), freeing hundreds of GB per server for KV offload or cutting host DRAM purchases.

title: Rotating nanostructured glass platter streams weights to batch inference
idea: In throughput-oriented batch inference the weight pass is a sequential scan of read-only data, which rotating media serve at the lowest cost per bit. A spinning fused-silica platter with laser-written multilevel nanostructures is read by a 10,000-element VCSEL/photodiode head array (~1 Gb/s each, ~10 Tb/s total), streaming a 70B FP8 model every ~60 ms, amortized over a batch of hundreds of sequences.
why: Weights leave DRAM entirely for batch jobs; the glass medium costs <$0.01/GB and needs no power to retain data.

title: Mainframe-style rack-wide content-addressed page sharing over CXL
idea: From mainframes that pack thousands of guests on one box: a CXL memory appliance hashes 4 KB pages from every host in a rack, keeps one copy of identical pages (OS images, libraries, model weights, container layers) and maps it read-only into each host, breaking sharing with copy-on-write.
why: Cross-host duplication is 10-30% in VM and container fleets and far higher for replicated weights; rack-wide dedup recovers it.

title: Rack-wide one-physical-copy rule via content-hashed CXL pages
idea: Imposed limit: no 4 KB page may exist twice in a rack. Each host's memory controller hashes read-only pages (kernel text, libraries, container layers, model weights) and swaps duplicates for pointers into a shared CXL-attached content-addressed pool, with copy-on-write on the first store.
why: VM and container fleets carry 15-40% duplicate pages, and per-host KSM misses duplicates that sit on different hosts; deduplicating across the rack recovers most of that capacity.

title: Capability-tagged immutable buffers enforce zero-copy across services
idea: Imposed limit: serialized copies of the same message are banned. Microservices pass read-only buffers through hardware capabilities (CHERI-style tagged pointers) that grant read rights across process boundaries, so RPC payloads, deserialized protobufs and caches all point at one physical buffer instead of 3-5 copies.
why: Copying and serialization take a sizable share of datacenter memory footprint and bandwidth; one-copy semantics could trim service heaps 10-25%.

title: x32 ABI, fixed: automatic per-heap 32-bit pointer compression in LLVM
idea: The x32 ABI (32-bit pointers on x86-64) died because every library and distro had to be rebuilt for a new ABI. Instead, an LLVM pass plus allocator places each data structure in a 4 GB 'pointer island' and rewrites interior pointers as 32-bit base-relative offsets (like Java compressed oops / V8 pointer compression), leaving the external ABI untouched.
why: Pointer-heavy workloads (graphs, B-trees, KV stores, compilers) shrink 20-40% in DRAM footprint without an ABI break.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory pool exploits frozen leakage for refresh-free density
idea: At 77 K, thermally activated junction leakage and GIDL fall by more than 10^6, stretching retention from 64 ms to hours. A shared DRAM pool in an LN2 bath can then use 2-3x smaller capacitors and no refresh, and it serves a whole rack over optical links.
why: Both the capacitor wall (fact 1) and refresh (fact 3) disappear, giving ~2x bits per wafer in the pooled tier.

title: Erlang-B trunk dimensioning for rack-pooled CXL memory
idea: Treat servers' memory peaks like telephone call traffic: the rack shares a CXL memory 'trunk' sized with Erlang-B for a 0.1% blocking target, and blocked requests overflow to compressed swap the way blocked calls overflowed to alternate routes. Each server keeps only its base load locally.
why: Per-server peak provisioning wastes the peak-to-mean gap; statistical multiplexing over 32-64 servers cuts rack DRAM 30-45%.

title: Rank/select engines enabling succinct trees and graphs in DRAM
idea: Information theory says an n-node tree needs only ~2n bits, yet pointer trees spend ~128n. Add rank/select and balanced-parentheses navigation units next to the memory controller so succinct encodings (LOUDS, BP, Elias-Fano adjacency lists) traverse in O(1) per hop at near-pointer speed.
why: 5-20x smaller indexes, tries, graphs and genomics structures, which are often DRAM-bound.

title: Pointerless graphs: succinct structures for national-scale analytics
idea: Po: data structures without pointers. Graph, trie and index workloads (knowledge graphs, genomics, search) are rebuilt on succinct encodings (rank/select bitvectors, wavelet trees, Elias-Fano adjacency) and queried in compressed form on domestic CPUs.
why: Succinct encodings approach information-theoretic size, 5-10x smaller than pointer-based graphs, so national datasets fit the limited U.S.-made DRAM.

title: Rank/select instructions for compressed-domain data structures
idea: Worsen: decompress everything into fat structures before touching it. Flip: add popcount-rank, select and wavelet-access instructions so succinct structures (wavelet trees, Elias-Fano lists, FM-indexes) are queried directly in compressed form at near-native speed.
why: Capacity: 3-10x smaller indexes, graphs and genomics data kept resident and queried without expanding them.

title: Decomposer line recovers known-good DRAM dies from e-waste
idea: Like fungi turning logs back into nutrients, a low-temperature depackaging and test line recovers known-good DRAM dies from scrapped phones, laptops and DIMMs and re-packages them on a passive organic interposer as heavily ECC-protected far-memory chiplets.
why: Scarce resources and U.S. manufacturability: domestic urban-mine bit supply with no front-end fab.

title: Hippocampal sleep replay distills old KV cache into memory tokens
idea: During idle accelerator slots (the analog of slow-wave sleep), a small consolidation network replays each long session's KV cache and distills spans of 64-256 tokens into 4-8 learned 'memory tokens' that reproduce their attention contribution; the originals are freed. Recent tokens stay verbatim (hippocampus) while old context lives as consolidated gist (neocortex).
why: Capacity: long-context KV is the largest inference DRAM consumer; claims 10-30x reduction on context older than a few thousand tokens.

title: Fused-silica diffractive plate performs the first vision layers optically
idea: Etch a learned phase mask into fused silica, which is stable far above 125 C, in front of each camera sensor. The first convolutional layers then happen as diffraction before photons reach the pixels, and the sensor outputs feature maps directly. Neither those weights nor their large early activations ever touch DRAM.
why: Early layers create the largest activation tensors, so removing them cuts ADAS vision DRAM 3-5x.

title: Integrate-and-fire checkpoints store only threshold-crossing activations
idea: Saved activations for backprop are recorded like spikes: each neuron accumulates its value against a membrane threshold and only crossings are written as (index, quantized value) events; dense tensors are never materialized and are reconstructed from events plus a leak model during the backward pass.
why: Training activation memory: 4-10x fewer bytes for sparsely activated layers (ReLU-family, MoE).

title: Backprop activations stored as random-projection sketches
idea: Worsen: keep every layer's full activation tensor for the backward pass. Flip: store a seeded random projection (sketch) of each activation at 1/8 to 1/16 size and compute weight gradients from the sketch, regenerating the projection matrix from its seed.
why: Capacity: 8-16x smaller activation memory in training with small, unbiased gradient noise.

title: Fourier lens compresses training activation checkpoints at light speed
idea: Activation tiles saved for backprop are loaded onto a spatial light modulator, and a lens computes their 2D Fourier transform in one pass. A thresholding camera keeps only the high-energy coefficients (JPEG-style) for storage. Inverse optics, or a cheap digital IFFT, restores them during the backward pass.
why: Activations are 60-80% of training memory. Lossy 8-20x compression with a free transform shrinks the HBM requirement (facts 5, 6).

title: Bit-exact integer reversible transformers erase the activation stash
idea: Imposed limit: training may store activations for only one layer. Residual blocks use invertible coupling and run in fixed-point integer arithmetic, so the backward pass rebuilds each layer's input exactly, with no floating-point drift, and no activation stack is stored.
why: Activations dominate training memory at long sequence lengths; making activation memory independent of depth cuts training DRAM/HBM 3-10x for about 1.3-1.5x more compute.

title: Attention computed inside SSD controllers, only outputs returned
idea: Reverse data-to-compute for KV: the host sends the query vector to computational SSDs whose controllers run dot-products and softmax-weighted sums over KV stored in NAND, returning only the partial output vector and its normalizer.
why: KV never enters DRAM: KV capacity moves to NAND at ~1/10 the cost per bit, and PCIe traffic per step falls from GBs to KBs.

title: Succinct filters plus on-flash learned index shrink key-value indexes
idea: Combine ribbon/cuckoo filters with a learned on-flash index: a DRAM-resident filter (~1 byte per key) answers whether a key exists and in which segment, and a learned model stored on the SSD locates the record in one read, replacing full in-DRAM hash indexes.
why: Index DRAM falls from ~16-40 bytes per key to ~1-2 bytes per key for billion-key stores, using only commodity DUV-made SSDs.

title: Tensor-train embedding cores with a full-precision hot-ID cache
idea: Box: factorization × recommendation model × embedding row × lookup-time reconstruction × TT cores + hot-row cache. Huge embedding tables become tensor-train cores reconstructed per lookup, with the hottest ~1% of IDs cached at full precision.
why: Embedding tables are the biggest DRAM consumer in recommender fleets; TT plus hot cache shrinks them 10–100× at small accuracy cost.

title: JPEG for KV: DCT along the sequence axis, keep low frequencies
idea: Borrowed from JPEG: blocks of 64 consecutive tokens' keys/values per head are DCT-transformed along the token axis and only significant coefficients are stored with zig-zag run-length coding; attention for old blocks is computed directly in the frequency domain.
why: Adjacent tokens' KV are strongly correlated in many heads; 4-10x compression of older context with error confined to high-frequency detail.

title: Bubble major/minor loops in Co/Pt tracks rotate KV each token
idea: Revive the bubble chip's major/minor-loop layout with university-sputtered Co/Pt perpendicular films whose tracks are defined by ion irradiation: each minor loop holds one KV block as magnetic domains, all loops shift together under spin-orbit-torque current, and the whole KV cache passes the readout once per decode step.
why: Attention reads all KV every token, so a nonvolatile rotating store matches the access pattern with zero standby power and no refresh, moving long-context KV out of DRAM.

title: Delay-and-cluster scheduler groups requests by shared prefix
idea: Rearrange time: the router holds incoming requests for up to ~150 ms on purpose and releases them in batches grouped by system-prompt or document prefix to the same replica, so one prefix KV copy serves dozens of concurrent requests.
why: Prefix KV duplication across replicas disappears; KV memory per request falls 2-5x for templated workloads, using only scheduling software on installed GPUs.

title: eASIC structured ASIC, fixed: via-programmed ROM holding frozen weights
idea: Mask ROM died because every code change needed a full mask set, and eASIC's single-via customization never found volume. Store a frozen production model's weights in a via-programmable ROM fabric where one cheap non-EUV via mask encodes the bits, so a model update costs one mask and a two-week spin, not a new chip.
why: Weights at ~1 via per bit with no capacitor, refresh or DRAM; capital and energy per bit fall sharply for long-lived models.

title: Flikker, fixed: auto byte-plane split, MSBs in DRAM, LSBs offloaded
idea: Flikker/EnerJ approximate memory died on programmer annotation burden. The memory controller splits pages tagged as FP tensors by the ML framework's allocator (no annotations) into byte-planes: exponent/high-mantissa planes stay in DRAM, low-mantissa planes go to a CXL flash tier and are fetched only when a kernel requests full precision.
why: Most kernels run on the high planes, so weights/activations/optimizer state need ~50% of the DRAM: ~1.5-2x effective capacity.

title: Swap new DIMMs for retired DDR4 behind CXL expanders
idea: Substitute new wafers with recycled bits. DDR4 harvested from decommissioned servers is tested, binned and mounted on CXL expanders as a second memory tier in new DDR5 servers, and OS tiering places cold pages on it.
why: Hundreds of PB of DDR4 retire each year. Recycled DDR4 can supply 20-30% of new-server capacity at a fraction of the new-DIMM cost, with zero new wafers.

title: Origami: address unit stores structured matrices as their generators
idea: Fold rather than cut more paper: an address-transform unit in the memory controller treats tagged regions as symmetric, Toeplitz, circulant, banded or block-repeated, storing only the generating vector or triangle and computing (i,j) to generator offset on every access, so software still sees a dense matrix.
why: n^2 to n (or 2x for symmetric) storage for covariance, Hessian, convolution, positional-bias and kernel matrices in HPC and science codes, with no code rewrite.

title: Client-held encrypted session state for idle conversations
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of the server holding idle users' KV cache, ship a compressed (low-rank plus INT4), encrypted, integrity-tagged KV snapshot to the user's device after each turn and have the client return it with the next request; servers keep KV only for sessions that are generating right now.
why: Most chat sessions are idle >95% of wall time; moving idle KV onto client devices cuts server KV residency by roughly an order of magnitude for long-context chat.

title: Swap separate host and device copies for one unified package memory
idea: Substitute the host-DRAM plus device-HBM pair with one coherent physical pool on a CPU+accelerator package. Data loader buffers, pinned staging areas and checkpoints then exist once instead of twice.
why: An 8-GPU AI node carries 1-2 TB of host DRAM, much of it staging copies. Unifying cuts DRAM per node 20-40%.

title: Eliminate backprop activation storage via forward-only perturbation training
idea: Fine-tune with zeroth-order or forward-gradient estimates: two perturbed forward passes from a shared random seed estimate the gradient, so no activations are stored and memory equals the inference footprint.
why: Fine-tuning memory drops up to ~10x, so jobs that needed 8 GPUs of HBM fit on one.

title: Vacuum pack with crash foam: compress pages, fill freed space with ECC
idea: Packers shrink-wrap a product and fill the leftover box space with foam. Each 4 KB page in the compressed tier is compressed, and the freed bytes hold a long LDPC/BCH code sized to the space left over. At page scale, 1% raw BER needs about 15-23% parity, so any page that compresses 1.3x or better carries its own armor at no capacity cost. Incompressible pages go to a small protected tier.
why: Flaky 1%-BER cells deliver DRAM-grade reliability for the roughly 70% of pages that compress, with net capacity still about 1.6x thanks to the compression.

title: Player-piano rolls: stream weights from NAND page buffers to compute
idea: Borrowed from player pianos reading music straight off a moving roll: NAND dies with wide internal page buffers stream compressed weights over a short die-to-die bus directly into the NPU's SRAM line buffers, with dozens of planes interleaved so the read rate matches decode throughput and no DRAM staging exists.
why: Weights sit in NAND at ~1/10 the cost per bit of DRAM with zero refresh; DRAM shrinks to KV/activations, cutting capacity per inference server 5-10x.

title: Holographic page memory revived as optical attention-key correlator
idea: Revive 1970s Bell/RCA holographic page memory as a correlator: a context's key vectors are written as superimposed Fourier holograms in a rewritable photorefractive crystal, and illuminating it with the query on an SLM produces every query-key dot product at once on a photodetector array. Only the top-k value rows are then fetched from DRAM.
why: Keys are half the KV cache and every key is read every token; optical key storage halves KV DRAM and cuts key-read energy 10-100x at long context.

title: Mosaic tiles: embedding tables assembled from shared tile codebooks
idea: A mosaic renders any image from a few tile colours: store recommendation embedding rows as product-quantized codes into a few shared codebooks, decoded by a memory-side gather engine on a CXL device so the host still sees full-precision rows.
why: Recsys embedding tables reach TBs and are the largest DRAM consumer in ad datacenters; 8-16x compression.

title: Memory-controller-assisted marking lets GC heaps run near live size
idea: Garbage-collected heaps are sized at 2-3x live data because marking is slow and must stay ahead of allocation. The memory controller keeps a hardware mark bit per 16 B granule in spare ECC metadata and traces references in the background with a pointer-chasing engine, so the runtime can collect continuously and set headroom near 1.2x live.
why: Java, Go, .NET and JS heaps are a large share of cloud DRAM; cutting headroom from ~2.5x to ~1.2x frees 30-50% of that memory.

title: RAMDAC-style palettized tensors decoded by near-memory lookup tables
idea: TRIZ #32 Color changes: as 1990s VGA stored 8-bit palette indices instead of 24-bit color, store weights and embeddings as 3-4-bit indices into per-tensor 8-16-entry palettes learned by k-means; a 180 nm RAMDAC-like LUT chip on the memory path expands indices to FP16 on read.
why: 4-5x weight/embedding capacity vs FP16, with non-uniform levels that beat uniform INT4 accuracy and trivial decode logic.

title: Downhole-grade hot memory tiers let racks run waterless dry cooling
idea: From 200 C downhole tools that use SOI SRAM and ROM instead of leaky DRAM: shrink DRAM to a small hot-data cache on one cold plate and put bulk working state in 125-150 C-rated tiers (SOI SRAM, ROM weights, high-temperature NOR), so the rest of the rack runs at 60 C+ coolant and is cooled by dry coolers year-round in any climate.
why: Evaporative cooling is most of a datacenter's water (~1-2 L/kWh); hot-coolant dry cooling cuts on-site water >10x while DRAM per node falls 3-5x.

title: Revocable leases sell stranded VM memory to caches and batch jobs
idea: IFR: no installed DRAM bit is ever idle. Closest: hypervisors lease allocated-but-untouched guest memory (30-50% in public clouds) to caches and batch jobs under a 50 ms revocation contract; leased contents must be regenerable, so revocation simply drops them.
why: Recovers 20-40% of fleet DRAM with zero new chips.

title: Swap word-granularity tiering for bit-plane significance tiering
idea: Substitute the word with the bit-plane as the unit of placement. Tensors are stored transposed into bit-planes: the memory controller keeps the sign, exponent and top mantissa planes in DRAM and the low-order planes in CXL flash. Kernels compute first on the coarse planes and fetch low planes only for rows where an error-bound or confidence check fails.
why: Most ML reads need only 4-6 of 16 bits. Full values stay recoverable while DRAM-resident bits drop 2-3x for weights and activations, which improves cost per bit and energy per useful bit.

title: Transfluxor multi-aperture cells as analog non-destructive weight multipliers
idea: Revive RCA's 1955 transfluxor as electroplated planar permalloy elements with two apertures: the flux set around the small aperture is an analog weight level that gates how much of an input read pulse couples to the output winding, without disturbing the stored flux. Arrays of them perform weight-times-input in place.
why: Compute-in-memory with nonvolatile, unlimited-read magnetic weights, so weights are never fetched from DRAM; litho plus NiFe plating only.

title: Line-granular copy-on-write for forked inference workers
idea: Worsen: fork model servers and copy whole 4 KB or 2 MB pages on the first write. Flip: the controller tracks copy-on-write per 64 B line, so forked zygote workers share everything except the exact lines they mutate.
why: Capacity: 5-50x less memory duplication when spawning many workers from one warmed process (inference, serverless, browsers).

title: Salmon-run return: retired GPUs serve their HBM as KV pools
idea: Salmon die upstream and fertilize the forest; aging training GPUs are redeployed as dedicated KV-cache and expert-weight memory nodes over NVLink or RDMA, running only memory-serving firmware, so their HBM keeps supplying fast capacity to new accelerators instead of being shredded.
why: HBM supply: recovers 80+ GB of HBM per retired GPU, reducing new HBM needed for inference growth.

title: Crime-scene fingerprint: hybrid-bonded dedup base die under DRAM
idea: Fingerprints expose duplicates: a logic die hybrid-bonded (Cu-Cu anneal ~250-300 C) beneath a DRAM stack hashes every written line, keeps the fingerprint table in on-die SRAM and transparently stores duplicate lines once, exposing more logical than physical capacity to the host.
why: Virtualized and AI fleets show 20-40% duplicate lines; module-level dedup multiplies capacity 1.2-1.6x with assembly entirely below 400 C.

title: Copper hybrid bonds: stacked SRAM working set, DRAM demoted to cold store
idea: Cu-Cu hybrid bonding at <5 um pitch stacks four ~2 GB SRAM dies directly on the accelerator, so the hot working set (activations, hot KV, hot weights) is served at ~0.1-0.2 pJ/bit over vertical bonds; DRAM becomes a compressed write-back cold tier that can be cheaper LPDDR or flash-backed.
why: Most accesses drop from 3-15 pJ/bit to ~0.2 pJ/bit (15-50x lower energy per access), and per-device DRAM shrinks because DRAM no longer has to supply bandwidth, only capacity (energy, cost/bit).

title: DRAM-less SSDs via learned-index flash translation held in host
idea: IFR: storage needs no DRAM. Closest: host-managed/zoned SSDs whose logical-to-physical map is a piecewise-linear learned index 50-100x smaller than a page-level FTL table, kept in host DRAM, so SSD controllers ship without their ~1 GB/TB DRAM.
why: SSD-embedded DRAM is several percent of global DRAM bits; deleting most of it frees that supply for compute.

title: Court-stenographer chords: bigger tokens shrink KV until it fits SRAM
idea: Borrowed from stenotype machines that write whole words in one chord: the model uses latent multi-byte patch tokens (dynamic 8-16-byte patches) so each KV entry covers ~4x more text, and with latent low-rank KV projection a 32k-character context fits in on-die SRAM.
why: About 4x fewer KV entries times 4-8x smaller entries gives 16-32x less KV memory, small enough to live in SRAM with zero refresh.

title: Model-on-ROM: frozen weights etched in 40 nm mask ROM
idea: Inverts 'weights must live in rewritable memory': a frozen foundation model's INT4 weights are etched as mask ROM on existing 40 nm logic lines (~0.01 um2 per bit, so a 7B model needs ~280 mm2 of bitcells across a few dies) next to small accelerators, leaving all DRAM for KV and activations.
why: Removes weight DRAM entirely for long-lived deployed models, using mature, plentiful capacity and no DRAM wafers.

title: Thick-metal coil mask enabling TSV-free stacked dedup engine
idea: One added thick top-metal mask forms inductive-coupling coils on each DRAM die. The dies stack over a logic die with no TSVs, and that logic die runs a stack-wide 64 B content-addressed dedup engine with its hash index in SRAM. Duplicate lines across all 8 dies collapse into one physical copy, so dedup moves to the stack scale.
why: It avoids the HBM TSV tax (fact 6) while adding stack-scale dedup, for 1.3-2x effective capacity on VM, container and ML workloads.

title: Scheduler pairs jobs with anticorrelated memory peaks on shared slabs
idea: IFR: memory sized for total use, not for the sum of peaks. Closest: a cluster scheduler profiles each job's memory time series and co-locates anticorrelated pairs (checkpointing training vs diurnal inference, ETL vs serving) on one pooled DRAM slab with priority preemption to compressed swap.
why: Cuts provisioned DRAM 20-35% versus peak-sized allocation.

title: Negabytes: pay to free memory like utilities pay for negawatts
idea: Po: we pay people to un-buy memory. A federal program modeled on utility demand-side programs pays a verified $/GB-year for DRAM freed through software or architecture changes, measured by fleet telemetry; freed U.S.-made modules are bought back and redeployed to defense, research and domestic manufacturers.
why: Software efficiency is the cheapest domestic fab; a negabyte market could free 10-20% of installed U.S. DRAM within a few years at a fraction of fab capex.

title: Swap fixed model size for nested sub-models that shrink with memory
idea: Substitute a fixed footprint with an elastic one. Matryoshka-style transformers are trained so that narrower sub-models are prefixes of the full weight matrices (the first k heads and MLP columns); when memory is scarce the server unmaps the tail columns and serves the nested model, then re-expands when memory frees up.
why: Memory becomes a dial, not a hard requirement: 2-4x less resident weight memory at peak scarcity, so fleets can be provisioned for average rather than peak load.

title: Player piano: cold MoE experts computed inside 3D NAND
idea: Like a piano roll that plays the instrument directly, store rarely routed mixture-of-experts weights in 3D NAND with string-level analog multiply-accumulate (bitline current summing); the token vector goes to the NAND die and only the expert output returns, while hot experts stay in HBM.
why: MoE models leave 90%+ of parameters idle per token; computing the cold majority inside persistent NAND removes it from DRAM/HBM, ~5-10x less memory per model.

title: Landmark keys in DRAM, full KV blocks indexed on flash
idea: Inverts 'attention needs every past token resident': DRAM keeps one landmark key per 64-token block, and the full KV blocks sit on NVMe/CXL flash. Each decode step fetches only the top-k blocks whose landmarks score highest against the query.
why: Million-token contexts need DRAM for only ~2-5% of their KV: a 20-50x cut in KV DRAM.

title: Carbon-nanotube van der Waals memory runs code and weights in place
idea: Use CNT-fabric memory, which switches by van der Waals contact and is projected to retain data over 10 years well above 125 C, as byte-addressable main storage. OS images, maps and model weights then execute in place, removing the duplicate copy that is loaded from flash into DRAM at boot.
why: Eliminates the storage-to-DRAM double copy, for 40-60% less DRAM in ECUs plus instant-on.

title: InPhase holography, fixed: optical associative attention over KV keys
idea: InPhase's holographic disc died because tape and disk won archival storage. Use holography where it is unbeatable, parallel correlation: record key vectors as a volume hologram in a photorefractive crystal, shine the query as a beam, read correlation peaks on a camera to get top-k token indices, then fetch only those V vectors from flash.
why: Full keys never sit in DRAM/HBM; million-token attention fetches only top-k values, cutting KV memory >10x.

title: Photorefractive hologram recalls top-k keys so values stay offloaded
idea: All keys of a long context are written as superimposed holograms in an Fe:LiNbO3 crystal. Shining the current query beam reconstructs correlation peaks whose brightness equals each query-key dot product, all in parallel, and a camera picks the top-k tokens. Only those k values are fetched from flash or CXL, so the bulk KV never sits in DRAM.
why: Long-context KV caches of hundreds of GB move to cheap tiers, and DRAM holds only the top-k working set, roughly 10-50x less (facts 5, 8).

title: Eliminate parsed object trees: query JSON directly from raw bytes
idea: Services replace DOM-materializing JSON/protobuf parsers with SIMD on-demand cursors over the raw buffer (a structural-index tape), so no object tree is built in memory.
why: Parsed DOMs are 5-10x larger than their text; API gateways and log pipelines cut heap 3-8x.

title: Weight carousel: weights exist only in transit around an accelerator ring
idea: Po: the weights have no home. Model layers circulate continuously around an optical ring of accelerators; each node holds only a two-layer sliding window and applies it to its resident batch as the layer passes (data stays, weights move), so the cluster keeps one in-flight copy instead of one replica per data-parallel group.
why: Data-parallel inference replicates weights N times; the carousel cuts per-node weight memory roughly 20-60x for 80-layer models, trading DRAM for optical link bandwidth (fact 5).

title: Weight carousel rotates model shards around an accelerator ring
idea: IFR: one copy of the weights serves every chip at once. Closest: N accelerators each hold 1/N of the weights and continuously pass shards around the ring over chip-to-chip links; each chip applies the passing shard to its own batch, so the ring stores weights once instead of N times.
why: N-fold cut in replicated weight memory for data-parallel serving (8x on an 8-chip ring), paid for with link bandwidth that consumes no DRAM wafers.

title: Mitosis embeddings: tail IDs share rows until gradients disagree
idea: Imposed limit: embedding tables get 1% of their nominal size. New and rare IDs start out sharing one row with their cluster; the trainer tracks how much each ID's gradients disagree with its cluster mates and splits off a private row only when that ID keeps pulling away.
why: Recommendation embeddings occupy terabytes of DRAM and most rows are rarely touched; adaptive sharing could shrink tables 10-50x with little accuracy loss.

title: Foveated KV cache: precision decays with attention distance
idea: Like VR foveated rendering, keep full precision only where attention 'gazes' (recent tokens and tokens with high cumulative attention mass) and step other tokens down 16->8->4->2 bits as their attention mass fades, using a background demotion engine that re-encodes in place.
why: Most tokens are peripheral; averages 3-4 bits/value instead of 16, a 4-5x KV memory reduction with full quality where it matters.

title: Bytes-per-transaction disclosure standard for federal software procurement
idea: Inverts 'memory efficiency is a private engineering choice': a public benchmark and label, like Energy Star, reports peak and average DRAM per transaction for cloud services and enterprise software, and federal procurement favors top-quartile products.
why: Creates market pull for memory-lean software; cutting software footprint 20-30% equals years of new fab output, without a fab.

title: Zipper merge: approximate cross-request KV block deduplication
idea: Two lanes zip into one: hash every 16-token KV block with locality-sensitive hashing; when a new block lies within epsilon of a canonical block from any request (same RAG passage at a different offset, near-identical prompts), store a pointer plus a sparse int4 residual, applying a RoPE offset correction at read.
why: Exact prefix sharing misses non-prefix repeats; in RAG/agent fleets 30-70% of KV is near-duplicate, giving 2-4x KV capacity relief.

title: Token-ID memory: keep the words, regenerate the KV on demand
idea: Po: the program remembers nothing. Long-context sessions keep only token IDs (2 B/token) plus full K/V for a few anchor layers; when attention needs the others, their K/V are recomputed from the anchors in one batched pass on otherwise-idle compute.
why: KV is ~100-300 KB/token for large models; tokens plus 10-20% anchor layers cut KV memory 5-10x, buying memory with cheap FLOPs.

title: Client-carried KV cache: the user's device holds the server's memory
idea: Po: the user remembers the conversation, not the server. Between turns the server quantizes, entropy-codes, encrypts and MACs a session's KV cache and ships it to the user's phone/laptop/browser storage; the next request uploads it back, so the server holds zero KV for idle sessions.
why: Idle chat/agent sessions dominate KV residency; parking KV on billions of client devices cuts server DRAM/HBM for KV 5-20x, practical for contexts up to ~32k tokens on modern links.

title: Mobile-OS saved-instance-state: kernel discards rebuildable caches by cost
idea: Borrowed from Android, which kills background apps after they save compact state bundles: applications tag regions with a rebuild cost (ns/byte to recompute or re-fetch), and the kernel reclaims the lowest cost-per-byte regions first, signalling the app to rebuild lazily instead of swapping.
why: Caches (memoization, decompressed assets, JIT code) are 20-40% of server RAM; cost-aware discard can shrink provisioned DRAM 15-25% with predictable tails.

title: Eliminate SSD mapping DRAM fleet-wide with zoned flash placement
idea: Mandate zoned namespaces or flexible data placement across storage fleets, so the host writes log-structured and the SSD drops its page-level FTL map, which costs about 1 GB of DRAM per TB of flash.
why: Every exabyte of flash frees about 1 PB of DRAM, a large hidden demand cut while DRAM is 4x more expensive.
